newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac to announce early French election.
newsitem.headline: Chirac to announce early French election.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac, gambling his political future on the drive for a single European currency, was poised to call a snap parliamentary election nine months ahead of schedule in a broadcast to the nation on Monday.
His decision was seen as a bid to secure a safe, if probably sharply reduced, majority before taking fresh austerity measures to qualify France for European monetary union in 1999.

The president held mandatory consultations with Prime Minister Alain Juppe and the leaders of both houses of parliament on Monday morning and his office said he would make a television and radio address at 8 p.m. (1800 GMT).

National Assembly president Philippe Seguin confirmed he had been consulted under article 12 of the constitution, which gives the president the power to dissolve the lower house and call an election at 20 to 40 days' notice.
The only doubt was whether the two-round vote would be held on May 25 and June 1 or June 1 and 8. The earlier dates seemed more likely since Chirac was reported to want a short campaign.
The prospect of up to six weeks of political uncertainty with an outside chance of a left-wing victory gave the French financial markets the jitters, dealers said.
The franc, stocks and bonds all fell. The CAC-40 bourse index was down 1.20 percent in late trade on Monday after losing 2.69 percent last Friday as election speculation mounted.
The franc hit a one-month low of 3.3772 to the mark but was far from the panic level of 3.58 to the German currency reached on the day of Chirac's inauguration in May 1995.

A SOFRES institute opinion poll published by the daily Le Figaro suggested the ruling centre-right coalition, which controls 478 of the Assembly's 577 seats, would lose about 150 seats but keep a comfortable overall majority.
It forecast the extreme-right National Front would capture 14.6 percent of the vote but win only two or three seats.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis denied published reports that France was significantly adrift of the goal of cutting the public sector deficit to three percent of gross domestic product this year to qualify for EU economic and monetary union (EMU).
He told Europe 1 radio there were economic advantages to bringing forward the poll due next March, since political uncertainty was delaying investment decisions.

Industry Minister Franck Borotra said France needed to clear the decks ahead of key decisions on European integration, especially the selection in April or May 1998 of the first countries to qualify for a single European currency.
Pundits said Chirac wanted to get the election out of the way now rather than have to campaign next year at a time of unpopular austerity measures to qualify for the single currency.
Even before he fired the starter's gun, electioneering erupted in earnest on Sunday.
Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin said on television he would reject tougher austerity if it were required to meet the Maastricht treaty criteria for EMU.

Testing likely campaign themes, Jospin said an early poll would be "an admission of failure" by Juppe's government and the Left would offer an alternative based on shorter working hours and a revival of economic growth.
Jospin added that Chirac was worried about corruption probes rocking the ruling centre-right parties.
Communist party leader Robert Hue, who has demanded a referendum on a single currency, said Jospin's shift to a more critical stance on EMU was "undoubtedly a positive evolution".
The newspaper Le Monde said Chirac would justify the snap poll, the first to be called without a political crisis or a change of president, by the need to prepare France for the euro.
It said he would advocate reducing taxes and the role of the state -- two pledges he made in the 1995 presidential election, only to do the opposite after taking office.
The president's mandate will not be directly affected by the vote. Chirac has five more years to serve. But a left-wing victory could make him a premature lame duck.
